talks.title: "Expert Software Developers' Approach to Error" by Marian Petre (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Presents expert Software Developers Approach to Error by Marian Petre (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Marian Petre presents at Strange Loop 2022 on how expert software developers treat errors as opportunities rather than nuisances to be quickly swatted away.

Key Topics: Contrasting novice bug-fixing with expert approaches; errors as signals of deeper design flaws; recognizing bug clusters indicating systemic issues; and building cultures that embrace investigative debugging.

Technical Details: Petre describes how experts pause at anomalies, asking why rather than immediately patching. They examine dependencies and code structure to determine whether a bug indicates architectural misconceptions.

Takeaways: Expert developers use errors as learning inputs. Teams should cultivate curiosity about anomalies and resist pressure to ship quick fixes that mask underlying design problems.

talks.title: "Leveraging AI for Global Health" by África Periañez (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Presents leveraging AI for Global Health by África Periañez (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Global Health Context

África Periañez presents Bonsai, a Gates Foundation-funded organization bringing AI and machine learning to underserved communities. She cites stark health disparities—few doctors per capita in low-income countries and high preventable maternal mortality.

Behavioral Change Mission

Bonsai focuses on patient and provider engagement rather than raw prediction. Medication only helps if people take it and supplies exist locally, so the organization nudges behaviors toward better health outcomes using digital data.

Team Origins and Naming

Leadership backgrounds come from video-game machine learning that modeled individual player engagement. The name references Japanese benshi narrators who explained silent films—Bonsai aims to reveal what is hidden in health data.

Technical Platform

The platform organizes mobile-generated health data in low-connectivity regions, runs randomized trials and reinforcement-learning bandits, and builds recommendation, censoring, and forecasting models aimed at actionable interventions rather than prediction alone.

talks.title: "Stop Writing Dead Programs" by Jack Rusher (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Provides stop Writing Dead Programs by Jack Rusher (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Thesis

Jack Rusher's Strange Loop talk Stop Writing Dead Programs revives Seymour Papert's critique that computing education—and much of industry—still perpetuates irrational, historically inherited practices.

Punch-card era

Rusher recounts Fortran on punch cards, VAX batch jobs, 45-minute feedback loops, and terminal fear of dropped decks—hard in dumb ways unrelated to the actual problem, rewarding a priesthood with strong working memory.

Modern parallels

Today's long compile cycles, Docker/CI deploy waits, and cloud batch pipelines echo the same slow feedback; Docker exists partly because underlying stacks are overly complex.

Wrong mental model

Compile-run separation, linear single-threaded execution, and input-output-transformer programs poorly fit long-lived servers (1000-day uptimes) and rich GUI/event-driven systems we actually build.

Call to action

Mastering pointlessly hard workflows breeds pride in preserving them; Rusher urges abandoning dead program thinking for interactive, pragmatic development environments.

talks.title: "Programmable Ink" by Szymon Kaliski (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Discusses programmable Ink by Szymon Kaliski (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Dynamic Medium, Static Tools

Szymon Kaliski of Ink & Switch presents "Programmable Ink" at Strange Loop, questioning why digital drawing tools simulate paper instead of exploiting computation. Even sophisticated paint programs remain static regarding behavior—you cannot sketch seating charts that reorder when guests RSVP or bookshelves that parametrize after drawing.

## Tyranny of Formalisms

Professional design software demands pixel perfection early, pulling creators into rigid workflows. Kaliski argues the dynamic medium should blend sketching freedom with programmable behavior, avoiding premature commitment to final layouts.

## Spatial Queries Prototype

Demonstrations introduce spatial queries: canvas regions that ask which objects overlap them, returning live lists bound to UI properties. Drawing a checkbox near queried zones toggles state bidirectionally—mark removal clears lists; new marks repopulate them. Lists convert to Boolean conditions driving other elements.

## Research Toward Programmable Sketching

Programmable Ink prototypes explore how informal diagrams gain reactive logic without traditional coding. The research track targets creators who think visually first, enabling iterative exploration where hand-drawn structures carry executable semantics—a middle ground between whiteboards and production CAD systems.

talks.title: "A Distributed File System for Secure P2P Applications" by Brooklyn Zelenka (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Evaluates A Distributed File System for Secure P2P Applications by Brooklyn Zelenka (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Brooklyn Zelenka, co-founder and CTO of Fission, presents WNFS (Web Native File System)—a distributed file system for secure peer-to-peer applications built on local-first principles. The three-year project, initially dismissed as impossible, fundamentally inverts traditional server-centric architectures to let users own and control their data across multiple stores while operating offline-first.

## Motivation and Context
Zelenka argues that internet infrastructure has radically changed since the 1990s: clients are now powerful (e.g., iPhone chips), bandwidth is abundant but latency is the constraint, access is distributed globally, and data privacy is increasingly regulated. Yet software architecture remains trapped in the LAMP stack paradigm of centralized servers. WNFS applies newer data structures and leverages modern client capabilities to enable users to own their data, possess one or more stores, and load data into applications as needed—mirroring how native platforms manage resources.

## Four Core Properties
The system requires four properties: local-first Access Control, arbitrary metadata, mutability, and versioning. Each is essential; initial skeptics discover their necessity when exploring how to avoid them.

## Public File System: Content Addressing and Hashing
The foundation uses content addressing—hashing data (e.g., SHA-256) so that identical content produces identical hashes deterministically. This differs from traditional URL-based addressing (which is location-dependent). Content addresses enable deterministic naming across distributed systems, selective replication, and clean diffs. WNFS uses IPLD (Interplanetary Linked Data) format with bytes and links. A mutable pointer (DNS TXT records) decouples addressing from data structures, permitting updates, atomic writes, and rollbacks while preserving history.

## File System Structure
The layout includes: a root with owner information (public key), public content, encrypted data sections, and a sharing inbox. Public files are organized in Merkle trees: each file has a header (SDK-controlled), raw user data, and metadata; directories index files and subdirectories. Changes create new versions; shared unchanged blocks enable structural sharing. History is stored per file as a linear or branched sequence; revisions form a causal semi-lattice supporting merging. A tunable hash-based checkpoint mechanism accelerates diffs by identifying the last common ancestor across branching histories.

## Private File System: The Dark Forest
Encrypted data is organized in a CHAMP (Compact Hash Array Map Prefix tree)—an optimized hash-array map trie with branching factor 16, balancing efficient diffs and shallow trees. The structure is append-only, miracleized (identical structures have identical hashes), and concurrency-friendly. All leaves appear as random bits, enabling efficient merging via set union. Every block and file has a unique key, derived randomly and unrelated to hierarchy; this prevents key rotation from affecting unrelated files. Users decrypt blocks starting from one top key, progressively discovering the tree structure—no server is queried for access proofs.

## Temporal Cryptography and Access Control
Time is orthogonal to hierarchy. A key ratchet—repeatedly hashing a key to derive the next version's key—enables forward traversal in time but not backward. A skip ratchet permits efficient jumps. Granular access is provided by deriving keys: giving access to a specific file, directory, or time range creates zero-knowledge witnesses using RSA accumulators with quasi-commutativity. These accumulators hash path segments and version information together in an order-agnostic way (quasi-commutative), proving membership without revealing the path.

## Write Access and Lazy Rooting
Users with partial write access create updates unrooted to the top (because the top structure is unknown to them). These are lazily attached upward when someone with higher access integrates them, performing structural sharing and backlinks. Over time, the tree is collaboratively built from leaf to root.

## Path Privacy
To prevent correlation attacks (e.g., identifying legal vs. family documents), all file names and paths are encrypted. The system uses RSA accumulators to prove that a file name exists under a given parent without revealing either the hierarchy or the name itself—just opaque random bits and a witness.

## Technical Implementation
Originally written in TypeScript, WNFS is being rewritten in WebAssembly and Rust to target web and native applications. The system emphasizes that "all pipes are broken"—assuming data will be compromised, so encryption-at-rest and in-transit is mandatory. The API mirrors Unix commands (ls, mkdir, rm, mv) with additions for history, versioning, and merge semantics.

## Use Cases and Future Work
Deployed for web apps (Dropbox clones), tools for thought (TiddlyWiki), data science, and storage network integration. Future work includes completing the WebAssembly rewrite, building local-first encrypted collaborative data logs, expressing CRDTs as data log, improving IPFS networking (batching requests, maintaining peer connections), and deploying zero-knowledge proofs for certificate privacy. The project is driving standards via the Web Native File System working group spec.

## Key Takeaways
Content addressing and Merkle trees provide security and efficient caching. Structural sharing across versions saves space while preserving history and enabling rollbacks. Temporal cryptography separates time-based access from hierarchy. Path privacy via accumulators prevents correlation attacks. Lazy rooting enables offline-first collaboration. The system scales from local use to global peer-to-peer networks while maintaining end-to-end encryption and user data ownership.

talks.title: "Hodor: Detecting and Addressing Overload in LinkedIn Microservices" by Bryan Barkley
talks.teaser: Reviews hodor: Detecting and Addressing Overload in LinkedIn Microservices by Bryan Barkley and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Hodor (Holistic Overload Detection and Overload Remediation) is a system developed by LinkedIn to detect and address overload conditions in microservices. Deployed to approximately 1000 services in production for over a year, Hodor has engaged in hundreds of instances to protect services from becoming overloaded and unresponsive.

Barkley defines overload as when a process is asked to do more work than it can handle with available resources. Resources fall into two categories: physical (CPU, memory, disk IO, network bandwidth—hardware-limited) and virtual (thread pools, connection pools, file descriptors, semaphores—configurable thresholds that still cause system-wide overload when exceeded). Common scenarios include traffic spikes, back pressure from slow downstream services causing upstream accumulation, and noisy neighbors on the same host impacting each other.

Hodor uses three primary detectors with conservative thresholds. The Heartbeat/CPU Detector monitors JVM thread scheduling delays by running a background thread that sleeps for ~10ms; consistent violations (e.g., 28+ violations in 30 windows) indicate CPU starvation. The Garbage Collection Detector tracks time spent in GC and fires on thresholds like >11% GC time for >10 consecutive seconds, indicating potential GC death spirals. The Thread Pool Detector monitors Jetty thread pool queue wait times, flagging overload if requests wait >50ms for >10 consecutive seconds.

Hodor employs multiple load shedding strategies. Initial Adaptive Percentage approach dropped fixed traffic percentages but proved inefficient with varying patterns. Concurrency-Based strategy dynamically limits concurrent requests, better handling traffic fluctuations. Rate-Based with Traffic Tiering uses throughput as the metric with concurrency as the source of truth, enabling three-tier prioritization: optional (pre-fetches, offline systems—dropped first), degradable (user sees some impact), and non-degradable (critical paths—dropped last).

To prevent retry storms, Hodor maintains server-side histograms tracking retry counts and client-side budgets limiting retries. No retry storms have occurred with this system in place. Hodor deployed in batches with load shedding initially disabled, monitoring services for at least one week through production load tests before enabling. False positives arose from code behavior changes, fleet resizing, and poorly-tuned garbage collection; solutions included correlating detector firings with latency increases using moving average crossover algorithms.

Future roadmap includes additional detectors for Netty event loops and Parsec (LinkedIn's async execution engine); capacity engineering integration; intelligent auto-scaling accounting for cascading failures; and support for stateful and data systems. Hodor operates transparently at the framework level, requiring zero configuration from application teams.

talks.title: "Monad I Love You Now Get Out Of My Type System" by Gjeta Gjyshinca (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates monad practitioners Love You Now Get Out Of enterprise Type System by Gjeta Gjyshinca (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from Strange Loop 2022, Gjeta Gjyshinca (software developer at Morgan Stanley) examines the friction caused by using monadic concurrency abstractions, specifically Scala Futures, in large codebases. Working on a core platform supporting over 12 million lines of Scala and around 1,000 developers, the team aimed to decouple business logic from execution mechanics without forcing developers to deal with invasive type wrappers. Gjyshinca presents "Optimus," Morgan Stanley's internal managed runtime and platform that provides automatic concurrency, batching, and caching through simple annotations rather than type-level monadic acrobatics.

### Key Topics
- **Type-System Pollution via Futures**: In idiomatic Scala, introducing Futures transforms straightforward synchronous code into nested for-comprehensions, sequence-of-futures transformations, and complex nested types (such as `Future[Seq[Try[T]]]`). This leaks execution concerns into API signatures, damages readability, and complicates refactoring.
- **Limitations of Complex Functional Alternatives**: Advanced solutions like free monads and applicatives with effects push execution to the program boundaries via interpreters, but require significant category theory knowledge. In massive commercial codebases with developers from varied backgrounds (such as Java or quantitative finance), these approaches impede velocity and hiring.
- **The Analogy of Managed Runtimes**: Modern languages delegate memory management to runtimes via garbage collection rather than making pointers explicit in the type system (e.g., Eden pointers). Similarly, database engines use declarative languages like SQL to abstract away execution plans, concurrency, and locking without exposing them to user queries.
- **The Optimus Runtime and `@node`**: Optimus introduces the `@node` annotation in Scala. Marking a method with `@node` serves as a contract that the function is referentially transparent, allowing the runtime to handle concurrency, I/O batching, and caching automatically while keeping standard return types intact.

### Technical Details
- **Compile-Time Transformations**: The `@node` annotation triggers a Scala compiler plugin that uses `scala-async` techniques to transform annotated methods into state machines at compile time.
- **Runtime Scheduling & Batching**: At runtime, a custom scheduler executes these state machines. While awaiting I/O calls, the scheduler keeps the CPU active and aggregates independent database queries into batched operations, which significantly reduces network roundtrips.
- **Referential Transparency and Caching**: The runtime pairs referential transparency with append-only, bi-temporal data stores. Because querying at a fixed point in time guarantees deterministic results, Optimus transparently caches repeated queries without making redundant database calls.
- **Ecosystem Challenges & Tooling**: Omitting monadic types from method signatures means synchronous methods can inadvertently sit between `@node` calls, creating serialized execution bottlenecks. The platform addresses this through compiler warnings and profilers, while exploring lightweight JVM threads (Project Loom) to dispatch threads cleanly without blocking execution threads.

### Takeaways
Optimus demonstrates that concurrency, caching, and batching can be delegated to a smart runtime rather than burdening the type system. By relying on referential transparency guarantees via simple metadata (`@node`), teams can write concise, declarative business logic while achieving high-throughput, non-blocking parallel execution. Morgan Stanley has been working to open-source the platform (initially nicknamed Optimus Prime) after decoupling proprietary components and renaming packages.

talks.title: "Demystifying Privacy Preserving Computing" by Tejas Chopra (Strange Loop 2022)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates demystifying Privacy Preserving Computing by Tejas Chopra (Strange Loop 2022) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from Strange Loop 2022, Tejas Chopra, a senior software engineer at Netflix, demystifies privacy-preserving computation. The presentation explores how modern systems can perform meaningful computation and machine learning over private data without sacrificing confidentiality. Chopra outlines the tension between full privacy (no data sharing, zero utility) and full utility (unrestricted data exposure, zero privacy), motivating the need for middle-ground techniques that allow organizations to compute over sensitive data safely in domains like healthcare, cloud computing, and blockchain.

### Key Topics
Chopra categorizes privacy-preserving computation into four foundational paradigms:
- **Federated Learning:** Pushing machine learning models to edge devices (e.g., Apple Siri, Google keyboard autocompletion) rather than aggregating raw user data centrally. Devices train models locally and return only updated parameters.
- **Differential Privacy:** A formal mathematical framework that quantifies privacy loss (measured by epsilon) by ensuring the presence or absence of a single individual's record does not significantly alter aggregate query results, typically achieved by injecting calibrated noise.
- **Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC):** Protocols enabling multiple parties to jointly evaluate functions across distributed secret shares without revealing private inputs to any participant, often leveraging Shamir's Secret Sharing.
- **Homomorphic Encryption:** Cryptographic schemes allowing mathematical operations directly on encrypted ciphertexts, producing an encrypted result that decrypts to the plaintext answer.

### Technical Details
- **Federated Learning Trade-offs:** While compliant with privacy regulations like GDPR, it faces device-level compute disparities and "leaky abstractions," where adversaries can reverse-engineer models or infer sensitive data by sniffing updated parameters.
- **Differential Privacy & Epsilon:** Differential privacy bounds individual impact through an epsilon (ε) threshold. While used by organizations like the U.S. Census Bureau (2020), Google Chrome, and Microsoft, researchers identified issues with transparency, citing cases where Apple utilized very high epsilon values that leaked more privacy than anticipated.
- **SMPC & Shamir's Secret Sharing:** SMPC uses polynomial interpolation where a degree-t polynomial hides a secret at $x=0$. It requires at least $t+1$ points to reconstruct the secret, making it information-theoretically secure against unbounded or quantum computing attacks. However, SMPC suffers from high communication latency among nodes and vulnerability to colluding or malicious parties.
- **Homomorphic Encryption Challenges:** Schemes span partial (limited operations), somewhat (limited depth due to accumulating noise), and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). FHE focuses primarily on addition and multiplication, analogous to universal logic gates. IBM's HElib historically ran a trillion times slower than plaintext (reduced to ~75x slower), while Microsoft developed the SEAL library. Noise accumulation remains the central technical challenge during multiplication, requiring noise-resetting mechanisms.
- **Blockchain and Zero-Knowledge Proofs:** During the Q&A, Chopra highlights privacy gaps in public ledgers, noting privacy blockchains like Zcash transitioning from ZK-SNARKs (which required complex trusted setup phases) toward ZK-STARKs to preserve transactional confidentiality.

### Takeaways
Privacy-preserving technologies are not a substitute for core security and authentication; they operate as authorization and data-protection layers. The current adoption of SMPC and FHE is constrained by high computational overhead, communication latency, poor interoperability, and lack of standardized benchmarking across libraries. The future of privacy-preserving systems lies in hybrid architectures—combining SMPC for distributed processing, FHE for encrypted computation, and differential privacy to quantify disclosure risks.

talks.summary:
## Overview

Shane and Vicki, software engineers at the New York Times, describe how they organized the largest union of tech workers in the country over two and a half years. While emphasizing that "there are no shortcuts in organizing"—requiring thousands of one-on-one conversations—they showcase how custom-built technology provided strategic speed boosts to their campaign.

## Key Technologies Built

**Bubble Chart Generator**: The team created a visualization tool to map union support across the organization. Starting with a spreadsheet tracking 600+ employees using a five-point assessment system (ranging from "all in" to "anti-union"), Shane wrote Python processors to feed data into D3 visualizations with color coding (green for pro-union, red for anti-union, gray for unassessed). Coworker Shea significantly improved the design by removing manager nodes, making the chart far more readable. This eventually evolved into an online interface for uploading CSVs.

**Website**: Built with Next.js and Netlify CMS, the website enabled both developers and non-developers to contribute content. It used static site generation deployed to Netlify's CDN for global availability and speed. The CMS proved accessible enough that people without coding experience could edit testimonials, FAQs with markdown support, and other content.

**Slack Avatar Generator**: Olav created a minimal web app (just static files, no server/database) that let members upload photos and automatically add a union frame. The simplicity sparked organic collaboration—other engineers and designers jumped in unprompted to enhance the tool, enabling live previews of different photos. During remote-only work, seeing widespread adoption in Slack channels became a powerful morale booster and visibility tool.

**Live Vote Count Tracker**: For the NLRB vote, the team added a real-time vote counter to their website using Firebase Realtime Database. During the actual vote, manually typed values were updated as envelopes were read (Shane admits to making one typo that showed they won by three times their actual margin). The tracker included confetti animation, activated by clicking a Tada emoji.

## Technical Approaches

The team prioritized accessibility and ease of contribution. They chose Next.js because most developers at the Times already knew React. Netlify CMS provided a user-friendly interface for non-technical contributors. All code was eventually open-sourced in a GitHub org for the News Guild of New York.

Organizing challenges shaped technical decisions: they manually collected employee names via a "quilting bee" Zoom calls rather than scraping the internal directory (to avoid drawing management attention prematurely). The Amazon Bessemer warehouse example illustrated why accurate org charts matter—a 4x discrepancy in expected warehouse size nearly derailed their campaign.

## Campaign Phases and Outcomes

The campaign involved three main phases: Stage 0 (building an organizing committee of ~10% of the eventual unit), pre-public organizing (conversations with everyone), and public operations (ongoing steward-led dialogue). Management declined voluntary recognition, so a formal NLRB vote occurred in early 2022, ultimately succeeding. The union then transitioned to contract negotiations.

## Key Takeaways

Despite all technological tools, the speakers emphasize that relationships built through thousands of direct conversations remain irreplaceable. Technology accelerates but cannot substitute human connection. Practical advice for remote organizing includes cold-calling with scripts, starting conversations with intrigue ("something not work-related"), and providing structure ("lesson plans" with themes and talking points) to empower less-experienced organizers. The union's data on member support is kept private for strategic reasons, especially during contract bargaining when priorities matter.
